metaDescription: Six food processors and choppers at or under $100, compared on bowl size, motor power, slicing discs and storage, with honest limits for each.
expertTake: The Hamilton Beach 10-cup with slicing and shredding discs is the most capable machine at or under $100, and the Hamilton Beach 8-cup with its large feed chute is the value pick. The Cuisinart FP-5 is the one for small kitchens that mostly chop and shred. If you only mince garlic and herbs, the Ninja Express Chop is all you need.
introParagraphs: A food processor is a motor base with a locking bowl and a spinning blade or disc. It chops, purees, slices and shreds in seconds, so it replaces a lot of knife work for salsa, slaw, hummus and pie crust.

Prices move, and the $100 cap in this guide reflects listing prices when it was last updated. At this tier the choices are about bowl size, whether you get slicing and shredding discs, and how much cabinet space you can give up.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 10-Cup Food Processor with Slice and Shred Discs
products.description:
This Hamilton Beach is the most complete machine here. A 10-cup bowl, a 450 watt motor and two attachments cover five jobs: slicing, shredding, chopping, mixing and puree. The standout is a built-in bowl scraper, which you move by hand to push food off the walls without stopping the machine to use a spatula.

The scraper is the practical feature, because chopped food and hummus climb the bowl wall and stall the blade. With it you can process thicker mixtures in one pass. Next to the 8-cup Hamilton Beach it adds two cups of capacity and the scraper, and it sits at the highest price tier of the six.

The bowl and lid wash on the top rack and the discs store with the unit. Treat 450W as a mid-weight motor: it handles cheese, carrots and hummus but not heavy dough. Process in batches and let the motor rest between them.
products.bestFor: Home cooks who want slicing, shredding and chopping in one reliable machine.
pros: Slice, shred, chop and puree in one set
cons: Highest price tier of the six
Large footprint on a small counter

products.name: Hamilton Beach 8-Cup Food Processor, Large Feed Chute, 450W
products.description:
This 8-cup Hamilton Beach shares the 450 watt motor of its bigger sibling at a lower price tier. The headline feature is a large feed chute that takes a whole block of cheese, which cuts prep time because you skip the pre-cutting step.

The chute is the real difference at this size. A wide opening means fewer cuts and faster slicing and shredding. The 8-cup bowl is large enough for most jobs and small enough for easy storage, according to the maker, and compared with the 10-cup model it lacks the built-in scraper.

Expect a conventional plastic bowl and lid that lock to the base. Wash on the top rack and hand wash the blades to keep them sharp. For most households, this is the sweet spot of size and price.
products.bestFor: Cooks who shred a lot of cheese and vegetables and want to skip pre-cutting.
pros: Large feed chute fits a block of cheese
450W motor at a lower price tier

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 8-Cup Food Processor, 450W, Stainless Blade
products.description:
BLACK+DECKER designs this around simple assembly. You set the bowl on the base and the lid acts as the locking mechanism, so there is no separate latch to align. A stainless steel S-blade chops and mixes, and the 8-cup bowl is large enough for salsa, nut butter and hummus.

At 450 watts it matches the Hamilton Beach models on paper. The difference is the lock design, which suits people who find twist-and-click bowls fiddly. It sits at the third-cheapest price tier here.

As always with 450W, make nut butter in short runs and pause to scrape the bowl, because the motor warms quickly. The maker lists attachments for slicing and shredding, so check what ships with your version. It is a no-fuss, widely supported brand.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the simplest lid-lock assembly in an 8-cup machine.
pros: Lid locks the bowl, so assembly is simple

products.name: Dual 8-Cup Bowl Food Processor, 2-Speed, Glass and Plastic

specList.label: Bowls
specList.value: One glass, one plastic, 8 cups each

products.description:
This model sells you two bowls: one 8-cup glass and one 8-cup plastic. Having two lets you chop onions in one and meat in the other without washing in between. A two-speed press-and-hold control lets you pick low for gentle chopping or high for puree.

Press-to-chop is similar to a pulse button, because the motor runs only while you hold the control, which gives you precise texture. The maker mentions mincing small batches of boneless meat. Unlike the Hamilton Beach models, it does not offer slicing and shredding discs, so it is a chopper at heart. It sits in the lower-middle price tier.

Glass resists odors and staining, which suits garlic and onions, but it is heavy and can break. The brand is less established, so keep the receipt. It is a good second bowl for a busy prep session.
products.bestFor: Cooks who chop onions, herbs and small batches of meat and want two bowls.
pros: Handles small batches of boneless meat

products.name: Cuisinart FP-5 5-Cup Chop and Shred Food Processor

specList.label: Blades
specList.value: Chop blade and reversible shred disc

specList.label: Storage
specList.value: Blade and disc nest in bowl

products.description:
Cuisinart limits this model to two jobs and does both well. A universal chopping blade handles salsa, breadcrumbs and quick mixes, and a reversible shredding disc handles cheese and vegetables. The 5-cup bowl keeps the footprint small.

Storage is the clever part, because the blade and disc nest inside the bowl between uses and the cord wraps into the base. That means the whole machine lives in one block in a drawer or cabinet. Compared with the 10-cup Hamilton Beach it has half the capacity and no slicing option, but it is quicker to set up and wash.

Cuisinart is an established brand, which matters for replacement parts. It sits at the second-highest price tier. Buy it for a small kitchen or a household of one or two.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens and households of one or two that mostly chop and shred.
pros: Blade and disc nest inside the bowl

products.name: Ninja Express Chop NJ100GR 16 oz Food Chopper, Pulse Button
products.description:
The Ninja Express Chop is a small chopper, not a full processor. A 16 oz bowl, stainless steel blades and a one-touch pulse setting mince garlic, onion and zest, grind spices and blend small amounts.

Pulse control is the key technique with a mini chopper, because short bursts give an even chop while holding the button turns herbs into paste. At 16 ounces, about two cups, the bowl is a tenth the size of the 10-cup Hamilton Beach. It cannot slice or shred, so treat it as a garlic and herb tool.

It is easy to wash and takes almost no storage. At the second-cheapest tier it is a sensible addition even if you already own a full-size processor. Buy it alone only if your cooking is small-batch.
products.bestFor: Anyone who wants to mince garlic, herbs and onions without pulling out a big machine.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The 10-cup Hamilton Beach and 8-cup models cover family cooking, while the 5-cup Cuisinart FP-5 suits one or two people and the 16 oz Ninja suits herbs. Rated capacity is a nominal figure; for liquids it is lower. A bowl that is too big wastes counter space and leaves small batches spread thin. As a rule of thumb, chopping works best when the bowl is a third to half full, and slicing or shredding fills it much less, so a 5-cup bowl handles about two cups of vegetables per pass. If you regularly prep for six or more people, size up rather than running many small batches.

A reversible disc turns a processor into a slaw and cheese machine. The Hamilton Beach pair and the Cuisinart FP-5 include discs, while the dual-bowl and Ninja models are choppers. If you grate cheese weekly, discs are the feature to pay for.

The 450W models handle cheese, carrots and hummus but struggle with stiff dough. Wattage matters less than blade sharpness and bowl shape. Under 300W stalls on dense loads. The giveaway of a struggling motor is a rising pitch and a smell of warm plastic, at which point you should stop and let it rest for several minutes. Cold ingredients and firm cheese are harder on the motor than soft vegetables, so cut hard blocks smaller or chill them less.

A large feed chute, as on the 8-cup Hamilton Beach, takes a block of cheese whole. Small chutes force you to cut food to size. Check the chute before you buy if you shred often. A wide chute also lets you feed a whole tomato or an onion half, though a pusher is essential for safety and should never be replaced by a hand or utensil. Pressing gently and evenly gives a cleaner shred than forcing food down.
The Cuisinart FP-5 nests its blade and disc in the bowl, which makes storage easy. Glass bowls resist odors but weigh more. Wash blades by hand to keep them sharp.

Pulse or press-to-chop control gives even texture, while holding the motor on makes paste. The dual-bowl and Ninja models use hold-to-run. Learn to pulse in short bursts for salsa. A good habit is to count one second per pulse and stop to check the texture after five or six, because the blade moves fast and the last few seconds change a chunky salsa into a soup. Drain wet ingredients such as tomatoes before processing for the same reason.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared which jobs each machine can do. The Hamilton Beach pair and the Cuisinart slice or shred, while the others chop. A wider range scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bowl and chute
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at bowl size and chute width. The 10-cup bowl with a scraper led, and the 8-cup large chute followed. The Ninja's 16 oz bowl suits small jobs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the stated wattage with caution. Three models list 450W, so differences came from design. We did not rank on watts alone.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and cleaning
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed footprint and nesting parts. The Cuisinart FP-5 stores everything in the bowl, and the dual-bowl model needs more room. Dishwasher notes on bowls counted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value at the $100 cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Every item has a live listing price at or below the cap, ranked in relative tiers. We rely on spec sheets and owner feedback patterns, not our own cooking. The Hamilton Beach 10-cup is the top tier and the Ninja the second cheapest.

cards.label: Full processor
cards.text: The Hamilton Beach and BLACK+DECKER models slice, shred and chop larger batches, but need cabinet space.

cards.label: Mini chopper
cards.text: The Ninja Express Chop mints garlic and herbs in seconds and stores in a drawer, but cannot slice or shred.

howToChoose.note: Pick the processor if you cook for a family; pick the mini if you only chop small amounts.

howToChoose.subheading: For Hummus and Nut Butter Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A motor of at least 450W, a bowl with a scraper or wide base and the willingness to work in short runs. Thick pastes strain small motors.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Hamilton Beach 10-cup has the scraper and 450W motor, and the BLACK+DECKER 8-cup is a lower-cost alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You shred and slice often and want a scraper, which points to the Hamilton Beach 10-cup. An established brand like Cuisinart also helps with parts.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You chop small amounts; the Ninja Express Chop or BLACK+DECKER 8-cup does it for less.

maintenance.why: Dishwasher heat and detergent dull edges. Dry them upright.
High heat can warp plastic. Keep them on the top rack.
The motor will not run if the lock is worn. Clean food from the tabs.
Never submerge it. A damp cloth keeps the buttons working.
Chipped or dull blades tear food. Replace them if you can.

faq.q: Do I need a full-size food processor?
faq.a: Only if you slice, shred and chop larger batches. For garlic and herbs, a mini chopper like the Ninja is enough. A full model replaces a lot of knife work.
A 450W motor, 8 to 10 cup bowl and basic discs. You do not get heavy dough power or a lifetime motor. Prices move, so the cap reflects listing prices at the time of the update.
Most budget models are not rated for bread dough, so check the manual. Pie crust works. Heavy dough strains a 450W motor.

faq.q: Why does my food spread unevenly?
faq.a: Overfilling and holding the motor on are the usual causes. Fill to the line and pulse in short bursts.
Glass resists odors and stains but weighs more and can break. Plastic is light and scratches. The dual-bowl model gives you one of each.
The motor base usually outlasts the bowl and lid. Hand wash blades and avoid overloading to extend life.
